frictionVectors.title: EU ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains significant bargaining power as a gas supplier to Europe, but European diversification efforts could gradually reduce its leverage. Sonatrach remains central to national control of hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA AND MOROCCO
frictionVectors.details: Rivalry with Morocco continues to shape defense spending, regional diplomacy, and infrastructure priorities. The dispute constrains Maghreb economic integration and increases exposure to external security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, China, and Gulf-linked investors are competing for influence over the Lobito Corridor and associated mineral supply chains. Angola can gain infrastructure and bargaining power, but risks becoming a transit platform for externally controlled extraction.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND DEBT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and heavy dependence on hydrocarbon revenues limit Luanda's fiscal room. Chinese-linked financing and international oil companies remain important to infrastructure and production, reducing full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER-BENIN PIPELINE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil export pipeline has become entangled in political tensions and border restrictions between the two countries. Its operation is strategically important to Benin's transit revenues and to Niger's access to global markets.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL MILITANT SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Northern Benin faces pressure from jihadist networks moving south from the Sahel. Security cooperation with regional and Western partners is expanding, but foreign support can create dependency and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: DE BEERS PARTNERSHIP RESET
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater local beneficiation in its relationship with De Beers. The renegotiation reflects stronger sovereign leverage but also exposes the economy to market and corporate retaliation risks.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL DIVERSIFICATION RACE
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to develop copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals are attracting foreign capital and strategic interest. Botswana retains regulatory leverage, but limited domestic processing capacity could reproduce extractive patterns.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NATIONALIZATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production, licensing, and marketing while challenging foreign mining influence. Weak oversight and insecurity could shift control toward opaque networks rather than durable public ownership.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's reliance on Russian-linked security assistance has reduced dependence on France and other Western partners. It also creates new exposure to opaque contracts, political influence, and possible concessions tied to mineral access.

highlights: Regional Balancing with Rwanda and the DRC

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked firms retain substantial influence over nickel, gold, and rare-mineral projects, while opaque licensing and weak enforcement limit Burundi's effective control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Burundi's military presence and security interests in eastern DRC create friction with Rwanda and expose cross-border trade and infrastructure to regional instability.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in Mindelo and Praia ports strengthens connectivity but raises concerns over long-term control of maritime logistics and strategic facilities.

frictionVectors.title: Undersea Cable and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's digital and maritime-security infrastructure relies heavily on European and U.S. partnerships, creating resilience benefits alongside external dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and industrial projects expand connectivity but increase debt, contractor, and strategic-dependence risks around major transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Chad-Cameroon Pipeline and Oil Rents
frictionVectors.details: The pipeline remains central to export revenues, yet foreign operators and transit arrangements capture significant value while environmental and local-governance disputes persist.

highlights: Mining Sovereignty Tied to Security Providers

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors and foreign intermediaries retain strong influence over mining zones, limiting transparency and the state's ability to secure full public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Dependency on External Force Protection
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-backed forces for regime security strengthens executive control but reduces policy autonomy and complicates relations with Western and regional partners.

highlights: Oil Revenues Anchor a Fragile State

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Petroleum Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains dependent on oil transported through Cameroon, leaving revenue security vulnerable to foreign operators, transit leverage, and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and External Security Influence
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan drives refugee, arms, and militia pressures across eastern Chad, while competing foreign security relationships constrain N'Djamena's strategic autonomy.

highlights: Mayotte dispute remains central to sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: MAYOTTE AND FRENCH INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and shaping Comoros' migration and maritime-security environment.

frictionVectors.title: LIMITED RESOURCE BASE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on remittances, imported energy, and external aid leaves the state vulnerable to outside financial and logistical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY AND REGIONAL PROXIES
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and suspected external backing continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, border trade, and mineral corridors.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt supply chains remain dominated by foreign capital, processors, and trading networks, limiting domestic value capture despite renegotiation efforts.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on offshore oil and foreign operators exposes sovereignty and public finances to external companies, price volatility, and opaque revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FUNDED INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and resource-linked financing expand connectivity but can constrain fiscal room and increase external influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CAPITAL AND PORT CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain prominent in ports, logistics, energy, and mining, creating persistent questions about domestic value capture and strategic oversight.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN BORDER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel continues to drive security cooperation and outside military involvement along northern transport and agricultural corridors.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND GREAT-POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of United States, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue but limits Djibouti's room for independent security policy.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEBT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt exposure and reliance on externally financed port and rail infrastructure increase vulnerability to foreign creditors and competition over access to Ethiopian trade.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Asset Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs have increased reliance on Gulf partners, the IMF, and asset sales, creating pressure over strategic land, ports, and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, while Egypt faces growing concern over downstream water availability and the limited leverage of existing negotiations.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output is squeezing state revenues and increasing pressure to attract foreign operators, infrastructure capital, and new offshore investment on less favorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing remain important to national infrastructure, giving external creditors influence while domestic governance keeps resource control highly centralized.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing regional and international security interests, while tensions with Ethiopia keep port access politically volatile.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects provide scarce foreign exchange but leave the state dependent on overseas mining firms, opaque contracting, and vulnerable export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport links, electricity arrangements, customs access, and investment, limiting its room for independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political Legitimacy Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and international scrutiny can complicate access to development finance and constrain the government's ability to mobilize domestic resources for infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's energy sovereignty but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operating rules, and downstream water security.

frictionVectors.title: Landlocked Logistics Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Djibouti for most maritime trade leaves Ethiopia vulnerable to freight costs, port politics, and regional bargaining over alternative access through Somaliland, Eritrea, or Kenya.

highlights: Military-led transition seeks tighter control over oil and manganese
Rail and port upgrades remain dependent on external capital

frictionVectors.title: Resource Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater national participation in oil, mining, and infrastructure projects, creating uncertainty for established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Transgabon Railway Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese exports rely heavily on the Transgabon railway, whose aging infrastructure and financing needs give external lenders and operators significant leverage over resource flows.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential security and trade partner
Tourism and port access limit strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Encirclement
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends on Senegal for regional transport, security coordination, and access to surrounding markets, creating persistent asymmetry in bilateral negotiations.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited port capacity, unreliable electricity, and dependence on imported fuel restrict sovereign economic control and leave infrastructure planning vulnerable to donor and foreign-investor priorities.

highlights: IMF-backed stabilization is rebuilding fiscal room
Gold and cocoa remain central but exposed to external pricing power

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages water systems and agricultural land while diverting gold value through opaque domestic and foreign-linked networks, challenging state enforcement and formalization efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Commodity Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on gold, cocoa, and offshore oil revenues constrain policy autonomy, while creditors and commodity buyers retain substantial influence over fiscal and trade decisions.

highlights: Simandou is becoming the country’s defining sovereignty test
Junta-led resource nationalism is colliding with infrastructure dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Control
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project depends on large foreign-led financing, rail, and port systems, raising concerns that Guinea may capture limited value relative to the scale of its strategic deposits.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Corridor Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign operators dominate much of the bauxite value chain, while expanding mines and transport corridors intensify land, environmental, and community tensions.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external buyers
Political instability weakens control over ports and maritime resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Capture
frictionVectors.details: Raw cashew exports generate limited domestic value, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to foreign traders, seasonal price shocks, and weak local processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and Trafficking Risks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested political authority complicate oversight of fishing waters, ports, and trafficking routes, increasing exposure to foreign commercial and illicit networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and dependence on external lenders constrain Nairobi's room to renegotiate major infrastructure and energy projects. Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing interests increasingly compete around transport corridors and ports.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa-Lamu competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed development around Mombasa and Lamu is tied to wider Indian Ocean competition. Delays, security costs, and uncertain commercial returns limit Kenya's control over these strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and hydropower are deeply integrated with South Africa's infrastructure and financing. Phase-related dam and tunnel development creates revenue opportunities but leaves Maseru dependent on Pretoria for access, pricing, and implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic generation and reliance on South African transport corridors reduce Lesotho's bargaining power. External contractors and lenders retain significant influence over major water and energy assets.

highlights: Rail and port access remain contested

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations, especially around Yekepa and Buchanan, give foreign investors substantial influence over rail, port, and fiscal decisions. Liberia's ability to capture value remains limited by concession terms and infrastructure financing needs.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridor bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The reopening and expansion of mining corridors is drawing competing interest from Western, Chinese, and regional firms. Infrastructure commitments are valuable, but they risk locking the state into long-term extractive arrangements.

highlights: Oil revenue remains divided by force

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities, armed groups, and local power brokers continue to influence fields, export terminals, and the National Oil Corporation. Production interruptions and blockades expose Libya's limited sovereign control over its core resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-energy competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and other external actors retain leverage through security partnerships, bases, and political relationships. Their presence affects oil routes, reconstruction contracts, and the balance between eastern and western institutions.

highlights: Nickel and cobalt draw strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Ambatovy strategic exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Ambatovy nickel-cobalt project links Madagascar's export earnings to foreign shareholders, global battery demand, and external infrastructure. Fiscal and environmental pressures complicate efforts to increase domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: QMM and coastal resource tensions
frictionVectors.details: Ilmenite mining and port operations around Fort Dauphin remain sensitive because of land, conservation, and local-benefit disputes. Foreign mining influence is amplified by Madagascar's limited transport and industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor restructuring are stabilizing the economy, but external lenders retain substantial leverage over fiscal and development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and mining bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity shortages constrain new uranium and rare-earth projects, increasing reliance on foreign capital, technology, and regional power imports.

highlights: Junta tightens control over strategic minerals

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining operators for larger state shares and stricter compliance, raising the risk of arbitration, production disruptions, and investor retreat.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked forces provide regime support but have not eliminated jihadist threats, while their presence increases diplomatic isolation and operational dependence on an external power.

highlights: Nouakchott balances China, Europe, and Gulf capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major fiscal and geopolitical gains, but production timing, revenue-sharing, and infrastructure dependence expose Mauritania to partner and market risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains central to export earnings, leaving the state vulnerable to foreign operators, commodity-price swings, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Diego Garcia implementation
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty transition over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens Mauritius's legal position, but the long-term operation of the Diego Garcia base remains strategically and politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutions but remains dependent on foreign investment, tourism, imported energy, and international financial access.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating control and investment in the territory, while legal challenges and opposition from Algeria and the Polisario Front continue to complicate external resource partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy stress
frictionVectors.details: Drought and aquifer depletion threaten agriculture and urban supply, increasing pressure for desalination, renewable-energy buildout, and foreign-financed infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Control
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain decisive influence over northern LNG development, limiting Mozambique's near-term bargaining power despite the project's strategic value.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and Offshore Security
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity in Cabo Delgado continues to raise costs and constrain state access, while foreign security support remains essential to protecting energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Energy Capital
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors dominate emerging oil, green-hydrogen, and critical-minerals projects, creating opportunities but also risks of weak domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water availability, transmission capacity, and port infrastructure could leave major projects dependent on external finance and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government is reducing Western influence and seeking Russian security backing, potentially exchanging one form of external dependence for another.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Export Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Border closures, sanctions exposure, and strained relations with regional neighbors threaten oil-export logistics and fiscal revenues despite stronger rhetoric on resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is expanding domestic refining and local-content capacity, but upstream financing, technology, and major infrastructure remain heavily tied to foreign firms.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Security
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, pipeline vandalism, and community conflict continue to erode state control over production and reduce public benefit from hydrocarbon wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Minerals Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's position as a major minerals-trading hub remains vulnerable to allegations that supply chains benefit from conflict-linked production in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, investment, and security cooperation strengthen Kigali's leverage, but dependence on external markets and diplomatic backing constrains fully independent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore blocks attract foreign energy firms, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. The government faces pressure to avoid opaque licensing and future debt-backed expectations.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies heavily on external partners for maritime surveillance and economic connectivity. Competition among European, Chinese, and Gulf-linked interests remains manageable but could narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: New hydrocarbon production offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, while authorities seek stronger local content, transparency, and state participation. Renegotiation pressures risk disputes with international operators and financing partners.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dakar and emerging deep-water logistics assets are strategically important to European, Gulf, Chinese, and regional investors. Debt exposure and concession terms remain central questions for long-term sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and limited monitoring capacity continue to test Seychelles' control over its vast maritime zone. The country is using conservation finance and blue-economy diplomacy to convert ecological assets into stronger bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY PARTNER DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external partners for maritime surveillance, port access, and counter-piracy support. India, France, the United States, China, and Gulf actors all have interests in the island's strategic position.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINERAL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mineral operations remain central to export earnings, but revenue volatility and concession structures limit domestic value capture. The government faces pressure to improve taxation, local processing, and community compensation.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE AND MULTILATERAL FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Road, energy, and mining infrastructure depends on a mix of Chinese capital, Gulf-linked investors, and multilateral lenders. Financing needs can weaken Freetown's negotiating position over strategic assets and procurement standards.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS AND RED SEA COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, China, and Western partners compete for influence over Somalia's ports, security institutions, and maritime infrastructure. Foreign-backed arrangements can provide revenue and protection while entrenching fragmented authority.

frictionVectors.title: SOMALILAND AND ETHIOPIA TENSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Disputes over Somaliland's external port and maritime arrangements continue to challenge Mogadishu's territorial claims and regional diplomacy. The issue intersects with Ethiopia's search for sea access and raises risks of proxy escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic failures at Transnet railways and ports continue to constrain mineral exports and weaken state control over strategic logistics. Private operators and foreign investors are gaining leverage as infrastructure reform accelerates.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals contest
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese processing links, Western supply-chain initiatives, and domestic beneficiation goals. Competition over platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth prospects is increasing external pressure on mining policy.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains almost entirely dependent on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to fighting, sabotage, and political leverage from Sudanese armed actors. Foreign oil operators and creditors retain substantial influence over production and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and patronage crisis
frictionVectors.details: Delayed political reforms and elite competition continue to divert public resources away from state-building. External security, oil, and aid relationships reinforce a rent-based system with limited sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of gold
frictionVectors.details: The SAF, RSF, and associated networks compete for mines, trading routes, and export channels, while foreign buyers and intermediaries capture much of the value. Gold revenues increasingly finance armed actors rather than national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure warfare
frictionVectors.details: Ports, refineries, pipelines, and agricultural corridors remain exposed to military disruption and external bargaining. Egypt, the UAE, Russia-linked interests, and other regional actors shape access to Sudanese infrastructure and commodities.

highlights: Mining reforms seek greater state value

frictionVectors.title: LNG sovereignty dilemma
frictionVectors.details: Planned offshore gas development could transform state revenues, but financing, technology, and offtake arrangements give international energy firms significant negotiating power. Delays reflect both commercial risk and Tanzania's effort to secure stronger domestic benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam port and central transport corridors attract competing Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western interests. Expanded infrastructure may improve national leverage, but long-term concessions could narrow policy autonomy if governance safeguards weaken.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's container and transshipment economy depends on foreign shipping, logistics, and financing networks. The port strengthens Togo's regional influence but leaves customs revenue and strategic connectivity sensitive to external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity near the northern border are increasing demands on security resources and transport infrastructure. Cross-border trade and external security partnerships could expand foreign influence over northern development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The European Union remains a critical source of financial and diplomatic support, giving it leverage over border control and migration policy. Tunis resists overt conditionality while relying on external assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity pressures, limiting strategic autonomy. Efforts to expand renewables are slowed by financing constraints and regulatory uncertainty.

highlights: Oil corridor advances under foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed East African Crude Oil Pipeline and upstream projects promise export revenue but leave Uganda exposed to foreign financing, legal pressure, and environmental criticism. Tanzania's transit role adds cross-border infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Strategic Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Chinese infrastructure lending and Western security cooperation provide essential capacity while narrowing policy flexibility. Kampala continues balancing competing external partners to preserve autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Contest
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater state oversight and domestic value addition in copper while courting Western, Gulf, and Chinese investors. Competition for strategic mining assets risks leaving the country dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on regional rail and port corridors through Tanzania, Mozambique, Namibia, and South Africa exposes copper exports to infrastructure and political disruptions. Power shortages also threaten mining productivity and industrial sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Mineral Access
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional actors seek alternative access. Limited domestic processing means Zimbabwe captures less value than its resource base could support.

frictionVectors.title: Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and currency instability constrain access to affordable capital and infrastructure finance. The government relies increasingly on politically flexible external partners, reducing bargaining power over strategic assets.
